subject: Geography
sub_topic: Glacial landforms — cirque, arête, moraine, fjord, drumlin

concepts.name: Cirque: Formation Mechanism and Morphological Characteristics
key_dimensions: Process of nivation, plucking, and abrasion in cirque formation — distinguishing which process dominates at which stage
Morphological features: headwall, rock basin (tarn lake), threshold/lip — and why a lip forms despite erosion
Distinction between a cirque, corrie, and cwm — same landform, different regional nomenclature (UPSC trap on terminology)
Conditions required: aspect (poleward-facing slopes in NH), altitude, and snow accumulation threshold

concepts.name: Cirque Evolution into Higher-Order Glacial Landforms
key_dimensions: How multiple cirques eroding back-to-back produce arêtes and horns — sequence of landscape evolution
Role of headward erosion and rotational sliding in deepening the cirque floor
Tarn lakes: formation after glacial retreat, why they are characteristically deep and cold
Cirque glacier vs valley glacier — scale, movement, and erosional capacity differences

concepts.name: Arête: Origin, Types, and Associated Landforms
key_dimensions: Formation as a knife-edged ridge between two parallel cirques eroding from opposite sides
Distinction between arête formed by two cirques vs. by two glacial valleys (U-shaped valleys) eroding laterally
Pyramidal peak (horn/matterhorn) as the logical endpoint when three or more cirques erode toward a common center — common UPSC confusion with arête
Real-world examples: Alps (Matterhorn), Himalayas — and why horns are rare in lower mountain ranges

concepts.name: Glacial Erosion Processes: Plucking vs. Abrasion
key_dimensions: Plucking (quarrying): freeze-thaw mechanism, role of basal meltwater pressure, produces angular debris
Abrasion: grinding action of debris-laden ice, produces fine rock flour and striations — smoother surfaces
Which process dominates in cirques (plucking at headwall) vs. valley floors (abrasion) — UPSC trap on spatial differentiation
Glacial striations as evidence of past glaciation direction — relevance to paleoclimatology and Prelims map questions

concepts.name: U-Shaped Valley (Glacial Trough): Formation and Contrast with V-Shaped Valley
key_dimensions: Transformation of a pre-existing V-shaped river valley into a U-shaped trough — why lateral and vertical erosion are both significant
Cross-profile characteristics: flat floor, steep sides — vs. V-valley's pointed floor and gentler sides
Hanging valleys: why tributary glaciers leave their valleys 'hanging' above the main trough (discharge/erosion power mismatch) — frequently tested
Fjord as a drowned U-shaped valley — the critical link between glacial trough and fjord formation

concepts.name: Fjord: Formation, Distribution, and Distinguishing Features
key_dimensions: Formation sequence: glacial over-deepening of U-shaped valley below sea level → glacial retreat → marine transgression
Why fjords have a shallow threshold (sill) at the mouth despite being deeply eroded inland — UPSC trap: ice loses erosive power near terminus
Global distribution pattern: Norway, Chile, New Zealand, Canada, Greenland — exclusively in high-latitude, tectonically active or formerly glaciated coastal areas
Distinction between fjord (glacial origin) and ria (fluvial/river valley drowned by sea) — a classic UPSC comparison trap
Ecological and economic significance: deep-water ports, aquaculture, tourism

concepts.name: Moraine: Types, Formation, and Spatial Positioning
key_dimensions: Classification: lateral, medial, terminal (end), ground, and recessional moraines — spatial logic of each type relative to glacier movement
Medial moraine formation: merger of two lateral moraines when two glaciers join — often confused with lateral moraine in MCQs
Terminal vs. recessional moraine: terminal marks maximum advance; recessional marks pauses during retreat — used to reconstruct glacial history
Ground moraine (till plain): unsorted, unstratified glacial till deposited beneath glacier — distinction from fluvioglacial sorted deposits

concepts.name: Drumlin: Morphology, Formation Controversy, and Spatial Patterns
key_dimensions: Morphology: elongated, asymmetric hill — blunt stoss end (up-glacier) and tapered lee end (down-glacier) — UPSC trap on which end faces the ice
Formation theories: subglacial deposition vs. erosion of pre-existing till — why no single theory is universally accepted
Swarms/fields of drumlins and their use in reconstructing ice flow direction — basket-of-eggs topography
Distinction from esker (linear, narrow, sinuous — fluvioglacial) and moraine — all are depositional but formed by different processes
Examples: Ireland (Clew Bay), North America (Great Lakes region)

concepts.name: Glacial Depositional Landforms: Sorted vs. Unsorted Deposits
key_dimensions: Till (unstratified, unsorted) deposited directly by ice vs. outwash (stratified, sorted) deposited by meltwater — the fundamental distinction
Outwash plain (sandur): braided stream deposits beyond terminal moraine — grain size decreases with distance from glacier
Kettles and kettle lakes: formed by melting of buried ice blocks within outwash — often confused with tarns (cirque lakes)
UPSC trap: moraines are till-based (unsorted); eskers, kames, and outwash plains are fluvioglacial (sorted)

concepts.name: Esker: Formation, Morphology, and Distinction from Drumlin
key_dimensions: Formation: deposition by subglacial or englacial meltwater streams within ice tunnels — sinuous, ridge-like form
Why eskers run perpendicular to moraines but parallel to ice flow direction
Economic significance: source of sand and gravel aggregates; used as natural roads in Scandinavia
Comparison with drumlin (depositional, subglacial, oval) and moraine (depositional, marginal/basal, irregular) — three-way UPSC comparison

concepts.name: Kame and Kame Terraces: Fluvioglacial Deposition
key_dimensions: Kame: irregular mound of stratified sand and gravel deposited by meltwater in contact with stagnant or dead ice
Kame terrace: formed along the margins of a valley glacier where meltwater streams deposit material between ice and valley wall
Distinction from moraine (unstratified till) and esker (linear vs. mound-like)
Collapse and pitting of kame surfaces after ice melt — leads to uneven, hummocky topography

concepts.name: Glacial Lakes: Types and Formation Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Tarn (corrie lake): in cirque basin after deglaciation — erosional origin
Kettle lake: in outwash plain from melting buried ice block — depositional/fluvioglacial context
Ribbon lake: in over-deepened section of glacial trough — elongated, deep
Proglacial lake: dammed by terminal moraine or ice margin — prone to sudden glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) — high current affairs relevance
UPSC trap: all four look similar on maps but have fundamentally different formation mechanisms

concepts.name: Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs): Mechanism and India Relevance
key_dimensions: Formation of moraine-dammed or ice-dammed proglacial lakes and conditions triggering sudden breach
Climate change linkage: accelerated glacial melt increasing GLOF frequency and magnitude
India-specific vulnerability: Himalayas (Uttarakhand, Sikkim — 2023 Teesta GLOF), northeast India
Distinction from cloudbursts and flash floods — UPSC often tests this in disaster management context

concepts.name: Pyramidal Peak (Horn/Matterhorn): Formation and Distinction from Arête
key_dimensions: Formation by three or more cirques eroding headward toward a common summit from different aspects
Why the resulting peak is sharp and pyramidal: frost action + plucking on all faces simultaneously
Arête (ridge) vs. horn (point): arête = two-cirque system; horn = three-or-more-cirque system — UPSC MCQ trap
Global examples: Matterhorn (Alps), K2 and other Himalayan peaks — and why horns indicate intense past glaciation

concepts.name: Roche Moutonnée: Asymmetric Bedrock Feature of Glacial Erosion
key_dimensions: Formation: smooth, gently sloping stoss side (abrasion-dominant, up-glacier) and steep, rough lee side (plucking-dominant)
Key diagnostic tool: asymmetry indicates direction of ice movement — used in paleoglaciology
UPSC trap: distinguish from drumlin — both are asymmetric, but roche moutonnée is erosional bedrock; drumlin is depositional sediment
Crag and tail: similar asymmetric feature but larger scale, with resistant rock (crag) and trail of softer till (tail) — Edinburgh Castle example

concepts.name: Periglacial Landforms: Freeze-Thaw Processes Beyond Ice Margins
key_dimensions: Periglacial zone: area adjacent to glaciers/ice sheets subject to intense freeze-thaw but not covered by ice
Patterned ground (stone polygons, stone stripes): frost heaving and sorting of sediments by size
Pingos: ice-cored hills in permafrost regions — open-system vs. closed-system pingo distinction
Solifluction: slow downslope flow of water-saturated soil over permafrost layer — significance for slope instability

concepts.name: Continental vs. Alpine (Mountain) Glaciation: Landform Differences
key_dimensions: Continental (ice sheet) glaciation: produces drumlins, ground moraine, eskers, kettles, outwash plains at broad scale — e.g., Canada, Scandinavia
Alpine glaciation: produces cirques, arêtes, horns, U-valleys, hanging valleys, fjords — confined by topography
Why alpine glaciation produces more dramatic erosional landforms while continental glaciation produces more extensive depositional landforms
UPSC trap: fjords are coastal features of continental glaciation zones (Scandinavia, Canada) but are formed by alpine-style valley glaciers — the conceptual bridge

concepts.name: Isostatic Rebound and Post-Glacial Landscape Changes
key_dimensions: Isostasy: crustal depression under ice sheet weight → slow uplift after deglaciation (isostatic rebound)
Evidence: raised beaches, submerged forests in formerly glaciated coasts of Scandinavia and Canada
Distinction from eustatic sea level change (global) vs. isostatic change (local/regional) — classic UPSC confusion point
Implications for fjord morphology, coastal landforms, and relative sea level — connects glaciology to coastal geomorphology

concepts.name: Glacial Mass Balance and Its Geomorphological Implications
key_dimensions: Accumulation zone vs. ablation zone: where net snow gain vs. net ice loss occurs — equilibrium line altitude (ELA)
How mass balance determines whether a glacier advances, retreats, or remains stationary — directly controls erosion/deposition patterns
Zone of fracture (upper) vs. zone of flow (lower): brittle crevasses above, plastic flow below — affects erosion mechanisms
Climate change impact: rising ELA → shrinking accumulation zones → reduced erosive power → long-term changes in glacial landform development

concepts.name: Glacial vs. Fluvial Landform Comparison: UPSC Overlap Traps
key_dimensions: V-valley (river) vs. U-valley (glacier): process, cross-section profile, and associated landforms — most frequently tested comparison
Delta (fluvial) vs. outwash plain (fluvioglacial): both involve sediment sorting by water, but context and scale differ
Ria (drowned river valley) vs. fjord (drowned glacial trough): both are coastal inlets but origin, depth profile, and sill presence differ
Oxbow lake (fluvial, meander cutoff) vs. tarn (glacial, cirque basin) vs. kettle lake (fluvioglacial) — three different lake types tested as one question
